transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess what brings me in is I can’t seem to get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. The cracks, the spots, the sagging… I feel like whenever I’m around bankers or county office folks, they’re staring right at it. My wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, but I can’t shake it.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly, like checking mirrors, picking at your skin, or trying to cover up certain areas to fix or hide these imperfections?

Yeah… I do. Before I go to a loan meeting or set up at a craft fair, I’ll check the bathroom mirror, then the truck mirror, sometimes more than once. I keep messing with my hat, turning it this way and that, trying to make my face look less bad. And I catch myself looking at my hands next to the younger workers’ hands, comparing them. It ends up eating up time I ought to be using on the farm.
Does this concern about how your face and hands look cause you a lot of stress or interfere with your work, relationships, or daily activities?

Yes, it does. I’ve missed calls with bankers because I couldn’t get myself looking… acceptable enough to sit down and talk with them. And I’ve put off farm decisions for the same reason. I also stopped agreeing to photos for the retreat and craft sales, even though I know that would help bring people in. It’s embarrassing, but it’s getting in the way.

latest_inference.note: The patient's preoccupation with perceived defects in their face and hands, repetitive behaviors like mirror checking and camouflaging, and significant impairment in daily functioning strongly support Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22). Other candidates like F40.00 (agoraphobia) and F32.9 (depressive disorder) are less consistent with the specific symptom pattern described.
